Q-learning: a table that tells you what to do

A table with one number per cell and move fills in on a cliff grid. Its largest numbers give the value of each cell and the move to make.

October 18, 202612 min read

Reinforcement learning, one idea at a timePart 1 of 5

Q-learning keeps one number for every cell and move of a grid, and you make the move with the largest number. The pinned drawing is the whole method. Scroll and it zooms to the part you are reading.

A grid of 4 rows and 12 columns. The start is bottom left, the flag is bottom right, and the cells between them are a cliff.

The update

Bellman optimality equation Sutton and Barto, Eq. 3.20

q∗(s,a)=E[ Rt+1+γmax⁡a′q∗(St+1,a′)∣  St=s, At=a]\begin{aligned} q_*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\,&R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(S_{t+1}, a') \\ &\Big|\; S_t = s,\ A_t = a\Big] \end{aligned} q∗​(s,a)=E[​Rt+1​+γa′max​q∗​(St+1​,a′)​St​=s, At​=a]​

Q-learning update Watkins 1989; Sutton and Barto, Eq. 6.8

Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α [ r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′)⏟target−Q(s,a)]\begin{aligned} Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\,\Big[\,&\underbrace{r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a')}_{\text{target}} \\ &- Q(s,a)\Big] \end{aligned} Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[​targetr+γa′max​Q(s′,a′)​​−Q(s,a)]​

a′a'a′ Any move in the next cell

The update is one sample of the equation, with your current QQQ in place of q∗q_*q∗​.

Q-learning, as in the recorded run (ε = 0.1, α = 0.5, γ = 0.99)
  1. Set Q(s, a) = 0 for every cell s and move a. Set s = start cell.
  2. Repeat for 10,000 updates:
  3. With probability ε pick a random move a. Otherwise pick a = argmax Q(s, ·), the first on a tie.
  4. Take a. Observe r and s′. A fall gives r = −100 and s′ = start.
  5. If s′ is the flag: target = r. Otherwise: target = r + γ · max Q(s′, ·).
  6. Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α · (target − Q(s, a))
  7. Set s = s′. After the flag, or after 200 steps, restart at the start cell.

Credit travels backward

Every number on the route is built from the number after it, so the cost of the flag spreads back to the start.

When it converges

∑kαk(s,a)=∞,∑kαk(s,a)2<∞⟹  Qk(s,a)→q∗(s,a) with probability 1, for every (s,a)\begin{aligned} &\sum_k \alpha_k(s,a) = \infty, \quad \sum_k \alpha_k(s,a)^2 < \infty \\ &\Longrightarrow\; Q_k(s,a) \to q_*(s,a) \ \text{with probability 1, for every }(s,a) \end{aligned} ​k∑​αk​(s,a)=∞,k∑​αk​(s,a)2<∞⟹Qk​(s,a)→q∗​(s,a) with probability 1, for every (s,a)​

Also needed: a table, every cell and move tried again and again, bounded rewards (Watkins and Dayan 1992, page 282).

The recorded run uses a fixed α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5, which this theorem does not cover. The grid has no randomness, and the route numbers settle anyway.

Pros and cons

Pros:

  • No model. It learns from moves and results.
  • Learns every step. No waiting for the episode to end.
  • Learns the best route while acting otherwise.
  • Readable. You can print the table.
  • Converges for small tables, under the conditions above.

Cons:

  • Rows grow with the situations.
  • Falls while exploring.
  • Slow to settle. Arrows took 1,998 updates, route numbers 10,000.
  • The max runs high on noisy numbers.
  • The tabular guarantee does not carry over to an arbitrary formula.
Source checks

Equation and section numbers are from Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, second edition. Watkins and Dayan is Q-learning, Machine Learning 8, pages 279 to 292, which I read as page images.

  • Notation. The book writes the reward after step ttt as Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​. The update is Eq. 6.8, and q∗q_*q∗​ is defined in Section 3.6 with Eq. 3.17 and Eq. 3.20.
  • Greedy readouts. Watkins and Dayan, pages 280 to 281: V∗(x)=max⁡aQ∗(x,a)V^*(x) = \max_a Q^*(x,a)V∗(x)=maxa​Q∗(x,a), and the policy that takes a maximizing action is optimal. Page 281 says early Q values may not reflect the policy they define.
  • Convergence. Page 282 gives the conditions: bounded rewards, learning rates in [0,1)[0,1)[0,1), the sum of the rates infinite, the sum of their squares finite. The abstract adds that all actions must be sampled repeatedly in all states, with discrete representation. I did not read the 1989 thesis.
  • Maximization bias. Sections 6.7 and Example 6.7. In the book the left action leads to many choices with mean −0.1. The game uses ten.
The recorded run: data, settings, command

The widget shows one recorded run, re-run so that its intermediate tables exist. The game's saved runs hold only the final table.

  • Source. Breaking Bellman, a small game I made, at commit 681cae3. I imported its RLA.run unchanged and wrapped the learner in a separate script only to record each update.
  • Settings. World cliff (4 by 12, step cost 1, fall cost 100, no slip), table, step size 0.5, discount 0.99, one random move in ten, 10,000 steps, seed 202. These are the game's careful-q settings. The learner acts, takes the step, then updates, as in the algorithm above.
  • Check. The final table equals the saved table of the recorded seed-202 run in all 192 entries.
  • Recorded. Full tables after updates 0, 1, 5, 20, 100, 185, 300, 1,000, 1,670, 2,000, 3,000 and 10,000, and every update from 1 to 10,000. The widget replays updates 1 to 400 and shows four later snapshots.
  • Command. SEED=202 node pilot-v2/snapshots.js > pilot-v2/snapshots-seed202.json, then node pilot-v2/make-widget-data.js. Every number in the checkpoint table comes from replaying the full update log (pilot-v3/verify_numbers.js). Exact values come from value iteration (5,000 sweeps, discount 0.99).
  • Greedy walk. It breaks ties in the order up, right, down, left, uses no random numbers, and stops after 40 steps. At 185 updates it never reaches the flag.
  • Falls. Replaying the log shows 4 falls were the table's own favorite move, all early. The other 167 were other moves, including all 150 after update 2,000 (pilot-v3/check_falls.js).

Exact numbers: mirage and cliff table

These are re-runs of settings the game already uses, with its own RLA.run at commit 681cae3.

  • Mirage. Right door reward 0. Left door reward 0, then ten machines with mean −0.1 and standard deviation 1. Table, random moves 0.1, step size 0.1, no discount, 600 steps per run, 300 runs (about 467 episodes each). Left share 85.0% in the first tenth, 11.3% in the last fifth, estimate −0.036 at the end. Random moves alone give about 5%. I did not run a version without the max, so the cause is the book's explanation.
  • Cliff table, twenty runs. Table, random moves 0.1, step size 0.5, discount 0.99, 10,000 steps. In all 20 runs the start cell held −12.2479 and the greedy walk took 13 steps. The 13 route numbers agreed with value iteration to better than 10−1310^{-13}10−13. In the 37 standable cells, the favorite move matched an optimal move in 34.5 cells on average. I did not examine why the rest differ. The number for a step off the route into the cliff was between −112.13 and −110.2, against an exact −112.13.
  • Seed 202. 33 of 37 cells have an optimal favorite move. The four that do not are (0,0), (0,1), (0,3) and (1,0). The largest gap to the exact value over 148 numbers is 2.68. The start cell was updated 767 times, row 2 cells 507 to 739 times, rows 0 and 1 cells 35 to 127 times.
How the clips were made

Each clip is a real recorded run drawn by a real browser with the game's own web/scenes.js at the same commit, unmodified. I replaced only the clock (30 frames per second) and encoded with ffmpeg (H.264). The run script and raw results are stored locally and are not published.
